children: By Terell Wright and Drew An-Pham

Has the economy gotten better or worse during President Trump's second term? There's no one answer, but Americans will decide for themselves when they go to the polls for the midterm elections next month.

Democrats are favored to win the majority in the House next year and Republicans can afford to lose no more than two seats to maintain outright control of the Senate, according to election forecasts. With pocketbook issues playing such an important role in how people vote, we dug through the numbers.

Inflation is rising but the labor market is relatively stable. Gas prices are up but so are 401(k) balances. The economy doesn't rest on one president or administration. But many voters say they are unhappy with where it is headed. A recent YouGov/Economist poll found that nearly half of Americans say the current state of the economy is poor, with only 20% describing it as excellent or good.
Here is a look inside Americans' wallets over the past two years.
A typical family of four, defined by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, shopping on a moderate-cost food plan spent 4.6% more in August than it did in January 2025.
Ground beef prices have risen since last year to $6.79 per pound from $5.55 per pound, largely because of declining U.S. cattle herd size and a severe drought that damaged grazing conditions.

Milk and chicken breasts have also slightly increased in the same period. It isn't all bad news: Egg prices have more than halved in cost to $2.27 a dozen from $4.95 a dozen in January 2025, when prices were high after bird flu that killed millions of hens. Bread prices have also slightly cooled from a year ago.
Overall, food prices rose by 4.4% since January 2025, outpacing overall annual inflation, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported.

Trump has often tied his economic performance to the stock market's upward trajectory. The stock market has been resilient since he returned to office last year, despite rockiness after the president's Liberation Day tariff announcements last spring, and the continuing U.S.-Iran war that he began earlier this year.
The S&P 500 index has risen 30%, including dividends, since the close before Inauguration Day to Friday's close, boosting average 401(k) and IRA balances.

In July, the government began investing $1,000 for babies born between Jan. 1, 2025 and Dec. 31, 2028, whose parents open Trump Accounts — the custodial individual retirement accounts for children with special rules until the year the child turns 18. They are initially invested in the State Street SPDR Portfolio S&P 500 ETF, a low-cost exchange-traded fund that tracks the performance of the S&P 500. It is up 2.7%, including dividends, between the accounts' launch and Friday's market close.

Median monthly mortgage payments for buyers fell a bit last year, but have since risen again to around record levels. And mortgage rates keep going up, a challenge to future buyers. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate hit 7.4% this month, the highest level of his second term.

Americans are still feeling the effects of home prices and mortgage rates rising dramatically over the past few years. Costs associated with owning a home such as electricity, home insurance and property tax have gone up in recent months as well.

Trump has attempted to address rising home costs, including signing an executive order earlier this year restricting large investors from buying single-family homes. Congress passed a multipronged housing law over the summer.

New vehicle prices have gone up roughly 4% since last January, according to Edmunds, an online car-shopping platform. Trump's rollout of a 25% tariff on imported automobiles and parts last year raised prices for consumers.
The prices of three-year-old and five-year-old used vehicles slipped in recent months, after surging following the tariff rollout.

Americans are shouldering bigger debt burdens. They are borrowing more to finance vehicles and stretching their terms to keep payments manageable. The average amount financed for a new car reached $44,729 in September, up roughly $3,000 from January 2025. That was driven by higher overall vehicle prices, reduced down payments and higher interest rates. Average loan terms for new cars have risen to 70.5 months, roughly a month longer than January 2025.

While on the campaign trail in 2024, Trump promised lower gas prices. The start of the war with Iran, which subsequently led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, has catapulted fuel and diesel prices for Americans. Drivers are paying 38% more for gas a gallon than they were since Trump's inauguration, as of Friday, according to the Oil Price Information Service.
Since the start of Trump's second term, diesel prices have risen by 71% to $6.25 a gallon, as of Friday.
Moody's Analytics Chief Economist Mark Zandi estimates that the war in Iran has cost the average American household more than $2,000.
